source: Lucas (2000) Semantic priming without association: a meta-analytic review
finding: Meta-analysis of 26 studies: priming between words related in meaning but not associated does exist, but it is small.
numbers: 116 observations, 26 studies, 2,243 subjects after correcting for repeated measures. Mean d = .26 semantic-only vs .51 associative (73 obs). By study: .30 vs .49. Subjects needed for 80% power: 188 semantic vs 72 associative.
quote: semantic priming can occur without association
limits: Pairs are mostly category coordinates. Heterogeneity was significant (chi2 = 43.09, 25 df, p < .02). Many included studies had low power. Hutchison 2003 later disputed whether the pairs were purely semantic.
agent_relevance: Meaning-only links give a weak lift; adding a direct association roughly doubles it. A retrieval scaffold should not expect plain topical closeness to help much without explicit links.

source: Lucas (2000) Semantic priming without association: a meta-analytic review
finding: Priming without association did not shrink in tasks that limit strategy, which argues against a purely strategic account.
numbers: Lexical decision d = .33 (45 obs); continuous LD .27 (16 obs); mixed-list LD .26 (23 obs); by study paired LD .39 (16 studies), mixed LD .28 (5), continuous .18 (6); naming only .16 (29 obs; .18 over 9 studies).
limits: Few studies per task cell (5 to 6 in some). Task, SOA and relatedness proportion did not clearly moderate, but power for moderators was low.
agent_relevance: The effect appears even when the task cannot use relatedness to decide. Points to a real, cheap, automatic association layer.

source: Hutchison (2003) Is semantic priming due to association strength or feature overlap? A microanalytic review
finding: Re-checked each study behind Lucas. Concluded automatic priming comes from both association strength and feature overlap, and not from category membership alone.
numbers: Verdicts: mediated associates give the strongest evidence for association-based priming. Functional associates, synonyms and antonyms support feature overlap. Category coordinates and perceptually similar items show no automatic priming in the visual modality.
quote: automatic priming appears to be due to both association strength and feature overlap
limits: Narrative review, no pooled effect size. Critics say the null for coordinates came from studies that did not control feature overlap.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of link exist: learned co-occurrence and shared features. A memory store for the agent needs both edge types and should not treat 'same category' as enough.

source: de Groot (1983) mediated priming, as reported in Hutchison (2003)
finding: Key failure for multi-link spreading: in standard lexical decision direct pairs primed (cow-milk) but mediated pairs (bull-milk) did not, across 7 experiments.
numbers: Exp 1 (from Hutchison Table 2): direct 26 ms vs neutral baseline, mediated 2 ms (n.s.); vs unrelated baseline direct 43 ms, mediated 19 ms.
limits: Read only through Hutchison's review, not the original paper. Later work shows mediated priming returns when strategies are removed.
agent_relevance: Activation passing across two links is fragile. Do not count on multi-hop spread unless the design makes it robust.

source: Hutchison (2003) Is semantic priming due to association strength or feature overlap? A microanalytic review
finding: Mediated priming is found when task or list context blocks strategic matching: continuous lexical decision, lists with only mediated items, pronunciation.
numbers: McNamara and Altarriba (1988), McKoon and Ratcliff (1992), Shelton and Martin (1992), Bennett and McEvoy (1999) found it. Chwilla and Kolk 2002: 25 ms (n.s.) in Exp 1, 32 ms (sig.) in Exp 2 after an all-unrelated list. McNamara found small effects even across two mediated items (mane-stripes).
limits: Chwilla, Kolk and Mulder (2000) found a different result. Effects are about 10 to 30 ms. Compound-cue and co-occurrence accounts can explain some of them.
agent_relevance: Multi-hop spread is real but small, and hidden when a strategy dominates. Fits the LLM result below: depth 2 helps, depth 3 to 4 is flat.

source: Hutchison (2003) Is semantic priming due to association strength or feature overlap? A microanalytic review
finding: Rival to spreading activation: mediated priming may come from co-occurrence or shared meaning, not links. McNamara tested this.
numbers: Mediated items with plausible shared semantics gave 8 ms and with none 10 ms; no relation between plausibility and effect size (r = -.017). Livesay and Burgess found no relation between priming strength and lexical co-occurrence.
limits: Evidence cited second-hand inside the review.
agent_relevance: Supports a true network mechanism over a pure similarity mechanism.

source: Hutchison et al. (2013) The Semantic Priming Project
finding: Largest priming database: 1,661 targets, 768 subjects at 4 universities, lexical decision and naming, SOA 200 and 1,200 ms, first-associate and other-associate primes.
numbers: First-associate lexical-decision priming was 26 ms (200 ms SOA) and 20 ms (1,200 ms). Earlier Hutchison et al. (2008) got 42 and 60 ms on 300 first associates. On 283 shared pairs: 43 and 61 ms vs 25 and 23 ms. z-score priming .37 and .44 vs .18 and .16. Priming did not change from first to last 400 trials (19 vs 18 ms LD; 6 vs 6 ms naming).
quote: We are unsure why this difference exists
limits: Authors could not explain the shrinkage; perhaps the mix of relation types and only half the trials being first associates. 831 trials per session.
agent_relevance: Realistic priming over the natural range of word pairs is about half the classic lab effect. Expect weaker real-world lift than the founding studies suggest.

source: Heyman, Hutchison, Storms (2016) Uncovering underlying processes of semantic priming by correlating item-level effects
finding: Item-level priming in lexical decision and naming correlates across tasks at the short SOA only, which fits a fast item-based spreading process rather than strategy.
numbers: 1,661 items. Cross-task r at 200 ms: .09 raw RT, .21 zRT, .17 residuals (all pairs); primary associates .10/.13/.11; other associates .09/.19/.17. At 1,200 ms: -.03 raw, .10 zRT, .06 residuals; raw RT t = -1.05 (p = .29) and -1.48 (p = .14).
quote: rapidly operating, item-based, relational characteristic such as spreading activation
limits: All correlations are low because within-task reliability of item priming is low (split-half Spearman-Brown, higher at short SOA).
agent_relevance: Priming per item is noisy. Any scaffold rule keyed to single-item association strength needs wide margins and tests on many items.

source: Neely (1977) semantic priming and retrieval from lexical memory, as described in Heyman et al. (2016)
finding: Splits priming into fast automatic spread (short SOA) and slower controlled expectancy plus retrospective matching (long SOA); the long-SOA part depends on task strategy.
numbers: Heyman et al. state expectancy needs an SOA over about 200 ms and retrospective semantic matching can inflate lexical-decision priming. No numbers taken from the original.
limits: Not opened. Attributed second-hand.
agent_relevance: Distinguish cheap automatic recall of neighbours from deliberate expectation. In our agent the second costs a model call and can bias.

source: Hutchison and Balota (2005) Decoupling semantic and associative information in false memories
finding: Test of association against meaning in false memory. Lists converging on one meaning vs on two meanings of a homograph, with associative strength to the lure equated.
numbers: 6 experiments. Veridical memory differed between list types, but false memory of the critical item did not, across blocked and mixed lists, 80, 200 and 1,200 ms per item, recall and recognition. In Exp 6 lures after one-meaning lists were judged more related.
quote: false memory in the DRM paradigm largely reflects lexical/associative activation
limits: Word lists only. Authors conclude false memory largely reflects lexical-associative activation.
agent_relevance: Associative activation alone can create confident false items. An agent that retrieves by spreading activation will also retrieve plausible but absent items; it needs a check before use.

source: Colombi and Strapparava (2025) Semantic Priming in GPT: Investigating LLMs Through a Cognitive Psychology Lens
finding: GPT-4o mini on Semantic Priming Project pairs inside masked sentences, scored by token log-probs. Priming appears only in the complete-case analysis.
numbers: 500 trials; 298 log-probs retrieved; 127 usable contrast pairs. Complete-case Wilcoxon significant (W = 1793.0, p < .05). Multiple imputation (201 of 500 missing, 40%): W = 441.0, p = .088, not significant.
limits: Heavy missing data from API log-prob limits and tokenisation. Not a clean human-like effect. No effect sizes in ms.
agent_relevance: Association strength in an LLM is only partly visible through API log-probs; do not infer a graph from them.

source: Shaki, Kraus, Wooldridge (2023) Cognitive Effects in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 shows semantic priming on Semantic Priming Project words in a text version of lexical decision, but only for some prompt formats.
numbers: 300 targets (100 each of 4, 5, 6 letters). Confidence with unrelated vs related prime: 4-letter sentence format .56 vs .76 (p < .001); 5-letter .62 vs .81; 6-letter .66 vs .81; question format .78 vs .85, .81 vs .85, .81 vs .85 (p = .004 to .0044); simple format .79 vs .74 (p = .0054, wrong direction), .79 vs .78 (p = .726), .78 vs .76 (p = .30).
limits: One old model, in-context prompt priming, not weight-level. Format dependent.
agent_relevance: Context words shape LLM output strongly. Retrieved text in the prompt primes the answer, so spreading-activation retrieval mostly decides which text we prime with.

source: SA-RAG authors (2026) Leveraging Spreading Activation for Improved Document Retrieval in Knowledge-Graph-Based RAG
finding: Spreading activation over a heterogeneous knowledge graph for multi-hop RAG, training-free. Alone it matches HippoRAG 2 with phi4; with chain-of-thought retrieval it is best in all four setups.
numbers: MuSiQue (100 q, phi4) EM/F1/correctness: Naive RAG .25/.36/46; HippoRAG 2 .32/.52/70; SA-RAG .40/.54/67; SA-RAG+CoT .44/.61/75. 2Wiki (phi4): Naive .36/.42/48; HippoRAG 2 .50/.62/76; SA-RAG .57/.66/76; SA-RAG+CoT .72/.78/87. gemma3 MuSiQue: HippoRAG 2 .31/.47/59; SA-RAG .35/.48/56; SA-RAG+CoT .43/.57/69. Claim: up to 10 points over HippoRAG 2, 25 to 39 points over Naive RAG.
limits: Only 100 random questions per benchmark; off-the-shelf bge-large cosine as link weights. With gemma3 HippoRAG 2 beat SA-RAG alone on both sets (2Wiki .58/.69/75 vs .50/.59/66); authors blame the reader model's reasoning.
agent_relevance: Direct test of our S3: spreading activation helps most when combined with iterative reasoning, and gains depend on the reader model.

source: SA-RAG authors (2026) Leveraging Spreading Activation for Improved Document Retrieval in Knowledge-Graph-Based RAG
finding: Iteration depth and decay were set on very little data.
numbers: Steps beyond three did not help the baseline; decay constant c = 0.4 chosen on about 10 questions.
limits: Tiny tuning set; not a proper sweep.
agent_relevance: Use shallow depth and moderate decay; avoid deep chains.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: Personalised PageRank (a form of spreading activation) over an open-IE knowledge graph beats flat dense retrieval on multi-hop sets, most on entity-heavy 2Wiki, not on HotpotQA.
numbers: Recall@2/@5: MuSiQue ColBERTv2 37.9/49.2 vs HippoRAG 40.9/51.9; 2Wiki 59.2/68.2 vs 70.7/89.1; HotpotQA 64.7/79.3 vs 60.5/77.7 (lower). Average 53.9/65.6 vs 57.4/72.9.
limits: Graph built with GPT-3.5 OpenIE; 48% of errors are NER limits; node-level context is dropped, which hurts HotpotQA; hyperparameters tuned on 100 MuSiQue training questions.
agent_relevance: Spreading activation wins when answers hang on named entities and loses where context matters. Keep a dense-retrieval path as fallback.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: Ablation: proper graph spread beats using only the query nodes; adding direct neighbours without spreading makes things worse.
numbers: Average R@2/R@5: query nodes only 57.4/72.9 (full method); query nodes plus neighbours without PPR 46.2/58.4; without node specificity 54.4/67.8; without synonymy edges 57.1/72.5 (but 2Wiki R@5 85.3 vs 89.1).
limits: Same single graph builder; limited variants.
agent_relevance: Naive one-step neighbour expansion hurts. Weighted, decaying spread is needed, as in the cognitive models.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: Largest gains are in getting all supporting passages at once, which needs multi-hop retrieval.
numbers: All-recall gap to ColBERTv2 at top 5 widens from 3% to 6% on MuSiQue and from 20% to 38% on 2Wiki. With IRCoT, HippoRAG (ColBERTv2) gives average R@5 78.2.
limits: Retrieval metric, not final answer accuracy; QA gains tracked retrieval gains.
agent_relevance: The benefit is completeness of a chain, which S3 needs before reasoning starts.

source: Query-Aware Spreading Activation for Multi-Hop Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs (2026)
finding: A semantic gate on each propagation step (cosine between query and node description) improves answers and speeds retrieval over uniform spread.
numbers: n = 1,000: MuSiQue F1 41.68 vs 34.27 without gate (+7.4), EM 32.8 vs 26.1; 2Wiki F1 55.00 vs 51.44 (+3.6). Latency at T = 3: 4.9x faster on 2Wiki (0.09 s vs 0.44 s), 1.5x faster on MuSiQue (1.45 s vs 2.16 s). Control n = 500: MuSiQue 46.71 vs 38.19, 2Wiki 55.91 vs 51.76.
limits: One generator (Gemini 2.5 Flash); baselines taken from other protocols; 95% CI about 0.04 on mean F1; arXiv preprint.
agent_relevance: Spread should be gated by relevance to the query: the engineering version of a threshold plus semantic filter.

source: Query-Aware Spreading Activation for Multi-Hop Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs (2026)
finding: Strong on MuSiQue but loses badly on 2Wiki to phrase-node graphs.
numbers: MuSiQue F1: GraphRAG 39.40, HippoRAG 38.33, QAFD-RAG 47.99, this method 41.68. 2Wiki F1: HippoRAG 70.33, QAFD-RAG 69.41, this method 55.00 (about 15 lower), LightRAG 8.20, GraphRAG 15.20.
limits: Authors explain the loss by a typed entity schema with no nodes for dates and nationalities, and by comparison questions where graph traversal adds little.
agent_relevance: Spread cannot reach facts that are not nodes. Node design sets the ceiling.

source: Query-Aware Spreading Activation for Multi-Hop Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs (2026)
finding: Depth and decay sweeps: 1 to 2 hops is the biggest change; beyond that gains vanish or reverse; decay hardly matters.
numbers: T 1 to 2 adds 18.8 F1 on 2Wiki and 12.7 on MuSiQue. 2Wiki T = 2, 3, 4 indistinguishable; MuSiQue T = 3 best, T = 4 slightly worse. Decay swept 0.3 to 1.0 changes F1 by 2.8 (2Wiki) and 4.0 (MuSiQue), inside the CI. Four steps doubles latency with no gain.
limits: One dataset pair and one model.
agent_relevance: Matches human data: a second link helps, more links add noise. Cap depth at 2 or 3.

source: SYNAPSE authors (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Unified episodic-semantic graph with spreading activation, decay, lateral inhibition and a fan-effect dilution, tested on LoCoMo long-conversation memory.
numbers: Weighted F1 40.5 vs Zep 39.7, MemoryOS 38.0, A-Mem 33.3, MemGPT 28.0, LoCoMo baseline 25.6. Multi-hop F1 35.7; temporal 50.1 vs A-Mem 45.9; adversarial 96.6 vs LoCoMo 69.2. Tokens 814 vs 16,910 (about 95% fewer); cost $0.24 vs $2.67 per 1k queries; latency 1.9 s.
limits: GPT-4o-mini backbone; several baselines taken from other reports; adversarial score depends on a tuned rejection gate; hybrid vector plus graph retrieval.
agent_relevance: A direct memory-for-agents use with a cheap store. The rejection gate is a useful guard idea.

source: SYNAPSE authors (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Mechanism ablation: each cognitive mechanism fixes one failure type. Fan effect (hub dilution) matters most for open-domain questions; decay matters most for time questions.
numbers: Avg F1 full 40.5. No fan effect 36.1 (open-domain 25.9 to 16.8). No node decay 30.7 (temporal 50.1 to 14.2). No lateral inhibition 39.4. No gating 40.3 but adversarial 96.6 to 67.2. Remove activation dynamics 30.5. Remove graph structure 32.9. Vectors only 25.2.
limits: Authors built and tuned the system; one benchmark (LoCoMo); no repeated runs reported.
agent_relevance: The fan effect from Anderson's ACT is a real fix for hub flooding. Include it when adding associative retrieval.

source: SYNAPSE authors (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Robustness: propagation depth is the most sensitive setting; on low-similarity questions the graph holds up better than the semantic-only baseline.
numbers: Authors state depth is most sensitive; A-Mem drops over 50% on the low-similarity subset while SYNAPSE drops under 8%; best top-k about 30 (range 20 to 40); raising the gate to 0.15 lifts adversarial F1 but raises false refusals from 2.1% to 4.2%.
limits: Self-reported, one benchmark, one backbone.
agent_relevance: Where the question uses different words than the stored note, links beat embeddings alone. Count refusal cost when gating.

source: Misra et al. (2020) BERT semantic priming, as relayed in a search summary of Lam et al. (2023)
finding: BERT shows semantic priming mainly when context does not constrain the word, and only for some relation types.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; relayed through a search result only.
agent_relevance: Priming-like effects fade when the context already predicts the answer.

source: Jumelet, Zuidema, Sinclair (2024) Do Language Models Exhibit Human-like Structural Priming Effects?
finding: Structural, not semantic, priming. Models show inverse-frequency effects but are more asymmetric and less consistent than humans.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; different kind of priming (syntax).
agent_relevance: Do not transfer structural priming claims to semantic spreading.

source: Collins and Loftus (1975) A spreading-activation theory of semantic processing
finding: Founding model: concepts are nodes; activation spreads along links, weaker with distance and time; separate lexical and semantic networks.
numbers: Not read; model description taken from Lucas (2000) and Hutchison (2003).
limits: Not opened. Model is hard to falsify since link strengths are free to fit any result.
agent_relevance: Gives a design for graph retrieval with decay and a threshold, but no predicted numbers.

source: Hutchison (2003) Is semantic priming due to association strength or feature overlap? A microanalytic review
finding: Several relation types were left undecided: collocates, episodic relatives, script relations.
numbers: Stated as unclear and needing more experiments.
limits: Review is from 2003; a search summary says Coane and Balota (2011) later found priming for direct or mediated associates without feature overlap (not opened).
agent_relevance: Do not assume script or episodic links prime like semantic links; test them as separate edge types.

source: Hutchison et al. (2013) The Semantic Priming Project
finding: Subjects also did reading tests and attentional-control tasks, so priming can be tied to ability. The database is meant to test which predictors (association, LSA, BEAGLE, feature overlap) explain priming.
numbers: 768 subjects with Woodcock-Johnson reading battery, three attentional-control tasks (Ospan, antisaccade, Stroop) and a morningness scale; largest single item effect 262 ms (shove-push, synonym, 200 ms SOA).
limits: The methods paper does not report the final variance analyses.
agent_relevance: Attention control and reading skill are the known moderators to log if we run similar tests on the agent.
